title: 2026-27 Detroit Red Wings: A Tale of Two Seasons
parts: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times…Who are we kidding? This year it’s likely just going to be the worst of times. Opening day for the Red Wings is upon us, and regardless of what the microcosm of events against a sub-par New York Rangers team turn out to be, it will likely do little to tell us what this season has in store for long-suffering fans.

This offseason could not have gone worse from a team-building or vibes perspective. At every fork in the road, we chose the wrong path, or at least the wrong time. Whatever you think of Steve Yzerman, whatever you think of Dylan Larkin, to bridge or not to bridge with Simon Edvinsson, the front office chose wrong or did not choose at all.

But at the end of the day, 20 skaters are dressing up tonight and going to give it everything they have. And it’s not just a scrap heap of a roster. Moritz Seider is a legitimate top-5 defenseman in the league. He actually graded out as the top defenseman in the league last year across several models, including this site’s model that takes into consideration its own ratio of actual and expected performance. Alex DeBrincat scored over 40 goals. Lucas Raymond seems to be just one or two seasons away from potentially cracking 90-100 points. John Gibson played an extended period of time as a top-3 goalie in the league last year.

When you look closely, you see the most capable goalie tandem the Red Wings have had in quite some time, and a better D-core (assuming Edvinsson gets signed soon and ramps up quickly) than the Red Wings have had in a longer time. But this forward group with Larkin is below average, and without him it’s hard to see how they can generate enough offense to do anything resembling a good hockey team. In the end, regardless of how inspired this team is to prove doubters wrong, this team is likely to miss the playoffs for an eleventh straight season.
Simulating the 2026-27 Detroit Red Wings Season

In an effort to steer away from my own pessimism and subjectivity, I decided to run some simulations. One thousand simulations to be exact. 500 simulations of how the year would go with Dylan Larkin, and 500 simulations without him. This simulation model utilizes advanced projections from Evolving Hockey as well as a system for incorporating over and under-slotting of players based on the expected strength of competition they are likely to face. This is especially helpful when considering the fact that Andrew Copp may very well be the 1C for this team. It will also try to paint an accurate picture of how much harder offense will be to come by for the top Red Wings line when there’s such a drop-off in quality for lines two through four. Teams will be able to pick their matchups against the top line and do whatever they want against the rest of the team.

For each version of the Red Wings season - with Larkin and without him - I will choose one simulation where the actual point total for that season matches the average point total across the 500 simulations. We will then explore what happened in those two seasons, how they team did, how the players did, whether or not any of the Red Wings received any awards consideration, and who broke out versus who underachieved. At the very end, I will give my personal prediction for the season. So without further ado, here we go.
Detroit Red Wings come up short while Dylan Larkin stays for the season

The vibes in Hockeytown were off all season. Interim GM Shawn Horcoff was unable to move Dylan Larkin, and the locker room had to deal with the drama for an entire year. By the time April came around, it was hard to find any positive energy among the players. And when it was all said and done, the Red Wings finished with 84 points, good enough for 8th place in the division and 15th place in the conference.

Ironically, Larkin had one of his healthiest seasons in recent memory playing 80 games and finished above the 30-goal threshold for a 6th season in a row. DeBrincat followed up his stellar 2025-26 campaign with another season above 80 points (83), but missed cracking the 40-goal mark by one. Raymond finished above a point per game with 79 in 76 games, and he even set a career high in goals with 33. To round out the stars of the Red Wings, Mo Seider set yet another career high in points with 65, good enough for third on the team and one above Larkin. He could not extend his iron man streak, however, as he missed two games.

When it comes to the recent additions of the team, it was really a case of two extremes. Viktor Arvidsson, who came via free agency, scored 27 goals and added 35 assists, good for 62 points. Keegan Kolesar, who the team targeted via trade had the worst +/- of all forwards on the team at -31 and could only account for 4 goals and 6 assists despite playing all 84 games.

For the youth movement, Emmitt Finnie continued his ascent into a top-6 role for the team, scoring 19 goals and adding 19 helpers. Marco Kasper had a slight bounce-back scoring 18 goals and registering 30 points. Michael Brandsegg-Nygard lit the lamp 12 times but did not play as responsible a two-way game as Todd McLellan hoped for with a -29 rating. Axel Sandin-Pellikka severely disappointed, scoring an inexcusable 1 goal in 60 games with a -28 rating. Nate Danielson also inexplicably scored 6 goals but failed to register a single assist. But the one who may have been the biggest letdown was Anton Johansson, who didn’t register a point in the 8 games he played on the team before being sent back down to Grand Rapids.

John Gibson and Daniil Tarasov were about as average a tandem as you could expect, with .898 and .897 SV% and 2.83 and 2.64 GAA respectively. Michal Postava was a bit of a bright spot, being called up for 6 games and posting a .925 SV% and a 2.5 GAA. Sadly, the team waited a bit too long to bring him up despite being out of playoff contention for a significant portion of the season.

From an advanced stats perspective, Lucas Raymond was not only the best player on the Red Wings, but also the 5th best player in the NHL with a W&W value of 95.7 out of 100, trailing only Nathan MacKinnon (98.4), Adam Fox (98.0), Connor McDavid (97.4), and Jason Robertson (96.3). Seider (93.4) was the second best Red Wing and the 4th best defenseman, again trailing Fox, Rasmus Dahlin (94.9), and Lane Hutson (93.6). Despite moving to the third line, Ben Chiarot produced the worst season on the Red Wings by a large margin, proving that it may be time to move on from him and hand the reins to Anton Johansson full-time going into the next season.

When it comes to league wide news, the Colorado Avalanche won the Presidents’ Trophy with 131 points on the season, but Mikko Rantanen again got the best of them, this time in the conference finals. The New York Rangers had a truly surprising bounce-back season, getting first place in the Metropolitan and making it all the way to the Finals where they eventually lost to the Dallas Stars. And in the end, Jason Robertson finally proved once and for all that he should be part of the Stars’ long-term plans, bringing home the Conn Smythe with 17 goals and 12 assists in 28 playoff games.

It may come as no surprise that the leader in the W&W value metric also took home the Hart Trophy. Nathan MacKinnon had a season to remember, winning the Ted Lindsay, Art Ross and Selke trophies in addition to the Hart. Jake Guentzel’s meager 43 goals was somehow enough to get the Rocket Richard, and Adam Fox won the Norris. Jakub Dobes of the Montreal Canadiens won the Vezina with a .929 SV% and a 1.96 GAA. And to round off the player awards, Viggo Bjorck won the Calder with 24 goals and 32 assists, narrowly edging out Porter Martone, but safely ahead of Gavin McKenna.

For the Red Wings players who received votes, Lucas Raymond (7th) and Alex DeBrincat (9th) both finished in the top 10 of the Ted Lindsay. DeBrincat also finished 4th in the Rocket Richard. Seider moved up one slot in Norris voting, finishing 4th this year. And finally, Raymond also came in 10th for the Selke and 7th for the Lady Byng.

If there is one way to look at this year, it’s that Raymond and Seider continued to take steps forward, and Raymond finally had the type of season that Red Wings fans have been waiting for. The only problem is, we are no closer to finding a solution at center, even if Dylan Larkin decides to stay for the remainder of his contract.
Without Larkin, at least we were still better than Toronto

So much for the Maple Leafs getting McKenna and then immediately bouncing back. Only Nashville and Calgary finished with worse point totals than the 74 that Auston Matthews and company mustered up. The Red Wings still finished 7th in the Atlantic, 15th in the East, and 28th in the league. But the only reason we didn’t do worse is because the defense held things down enough to cover up for our terrible offense.

There’s no way around it, the void Larkin left on the top line was more like a black hole. Sure, Andrew Copp put up 43 points centering DeBrincat and Raymond, but teams matched up so easily against the top-heavy first unit that DeBrincat could only get 59 points and Raymond 53 points. The only player who seemed to hold his own off the first line was newcomer Viktor Arvidsson who came in second on the team with 55 points.

The team could do nothing in the O-zone, tying for last with Nashville in goals with 221, and putting tremendous pressure on the defense due to such a lopsided time of possession. The defense performed admirably, all things considered. The team finished in 15th place in goals allowed, but had the 9th best expected goals allowed. This all despite having one of the worst SF:SA (shots for vs. shots allowed) ratios in the league.

It’s very difficult to find, but there were a few bright spots. The biggest has to be Nate Danielson. He finished with 12 goals and 14 assists, easily the best of the young players fighting for roster spots this year. Carter Mazur had a respectable 10 goals, and Brandsegg-Nygard finished with 8 goals and 8 assists. Marco Kasper and Emmitt Finnie were the 4th and 5th best Red Wings by value, but that’s a very low bar. Leaguewide, their seasons would be considered slightly above average.

The truly disappointing seasons belong to Axel Sandin-Pellikka, Anton Johansson, and William Wallinder. ASP got hurt after 21 games with a season-ending injury, greatly stunting his progression. Anton Johansson played so poorly in his first 2 games that he got sent down to Grand Rapids for the remainder of the season. Wallinder was waived after just 2 games as well. After clearing waivers, he also played out the rest of the season with Anton Johansson.

The team also waited too long to call up Michal Postava. Hindsight being 20/20, John Gibson should have been traded at the deadline. Instead, he was the worst of the three goalies with a .898 SV%, 2.77 GA, and a -3.7 goals saved above expected. Daniil Tarasov proved to be a nice offseason addition finishing with a .908 SV% and a 2.45 GAA. As hinted at earlier, Postava was the one who impressed. It was a small sample size, but in 4 games, he went 4-0-0 with a .931 SV%, 1.68 GAA and a 3.5 goals saved above expected.

Leaguewide, the Dallas Stars won the Presidents’ Trophy, but they got bounced early in the playoffs. This would be the year Tampa Bay returned to glory, beating Quinn Hughes and the Minnesota Wild for the Stanley Cup. Brandon Hagel was the main reason why, finishing the playoffs with 18 goals and grabbing the Conn Smythe.

Leon Draisaitl had quite the year, racking up tons of individual accolades. He finished with both the Hart and the Ted Lindsay, and he led the league in goals resulting in a Rocket Richard. The only player in his stratosphere was Nathan MacKinnon who was still able to pry away the Art Ross by a single point. Quinn Hughes started his work early, edging out Lane Hutson for the Norris trophy before his deep playoff run began. Connor Hellebuyck’s Vezina-winning season got Winnipeg back to the playoffs, despite a season-long standoff when the Jets did not honor his trade request. And finally Porter Martone was the unanimous winner of the Calder, finishing with 37 goals and 75 points, well above Anton Frondell’s 58 points.

It may come as no surprise, but not a single Red Wing got votes in any award category. It was a dark year and a horrible first step in the post-Dylan Larkin era. If there is one saving grace, it is that the Red Wings did not drop in the draft and held onto their 5th pick. You know you are in the Dead Wings 2.0 era when you are happy just to go chalk with the draft lottery.
Wes & Woodward Prediction

No matter how hard I look to find hope in the coming season, it still evades me. This year feels like it’s destined to go very poorly, and the only hope I actually have is that it won’t burn bridges with players like Seider and Raymond who would be integral to this team’s future success. That tells me all I need to know about where I actually stand on this year’s forecast.

First, some positives. I think that the year will give much needed extended looks at the young players in the Red Wings system. This is pivotal for players like Nate Danielson, Michael Brandsegg-Nygard, Carter Mazur, Anton Johansson and Axel Sandin-Pellikka who will start the year on the NHL roster. It’s also pivotal for players like Marco Kasper (who needs to turn things around after a sophomore slump) and Emmitt Finnie (who hopefully can build off a strong rookie campaign while avoiding a sophomore slump). But I want to also see some runway for non-roster players like Michal Postava and Carter Bear. This youth movement is likely going to be what it takes to move off of the “jerseys” who have been mainstays of the Red Wings roster over the last few years.

However, with a youth movement comes rookie mistakes. But that’s all palatable if progress is being made and an organization is turning a new leaf. A new leaf also needs to be turned in how the front office handles contract negotiations. Simon Edvinsson should not be nickeled and dimed. A little generosity can go a long way when it comes to how players feel within a locker room and how the team is perceived by other players outside of the locker room. If, by some miracle, the front office can salvage this negotiation process with Edvinsson and get an extension done with DeBrincat in addition to the positives that come from a youth movement, then I feel positive about the trajectory of the team moving forward regardless of how this year shakes out.

With all that additional context taken care of, I believe the models were overly generous to each version of the Red Wings’ season. I think Larkin will be gone before December. I also think Justin Faulk will be moved by the deadline. I also think it’s reasonable to believe that this front office may trade John Gibson’s expiring contract and move Postava up to the NHL forming a Tarasov-Postava tandem for a significant portion of the season.
All of that amounts to 75 points and the following placements:

• 8th place in the Atlantic
  • 15th place in the East
  • 29th place in the league

I am going to make an even bolder prediction when I say that the Red Wings will get some draft luck and pick 2nd in the upcoming draft. They’ll miss out on Landon DuPont, and a projected 2030 arrival time for Nazar Privalov will scare them off. The legacy of drafting Swedish players will land them to trade down a couple slots to pick Milan Sundström.
I’ll see all of you again for next year’s projection when we find out just how wrong I was every step of the way - not so unlike this Red Wings organization.
